name: GHK-Cu

b.x: At least 4,000 human genes. That's how many GHK-Cu raises or lowers in gene expression data analyzed by Pickart's group ([PMID 26236730](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26236730/)) [1]. The GHK-Cu peptide (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine copper(II), also written GHK:Cu or copper tripeptide-1) is a naturally occurring copper peptide found in human plasma, saliva, and urine. Plasma levels sit around 200 ng/mL at age 20 and drop to roughly 80 ng/mL by age 60. The mechanism is broad. GHK-Cu upregulates collagen I, III, and V synthesis, boosts elastin and decorin production, and recruits immune and endothelial cells to damaged tissue. The copper ion itself is required for enzymatic processes in wound remodeling. In 2024, Bian and colleagues confirmed anti-fibrotic activity in silicosis mice and found lower plasma GHK in silicosis patients [2]. Its research now reaches past skin. In practice, two routes dominate. Topical formulations (1 to 3% concentration) have cosmetic safety data going back decades; small clinical trials (n = 41 to 71) showed improved skin density and fine line reduction. Injectable use (0.5 to 2 mg/day subcutaneous) has no published dose-finding trial in humans but has one of the largest community evidence bases of any anti-aging peptide. Reports across r/Peptides, r/Biohackers, and practitioner networks describe improved skin firmness by weeks four to six; sentiment runs at 4.2 out of 5. The honest limitation: all mechanistic data is in vitro or murine. Pro-angiogenic activity flagged by the NCI raises an unresolved theoretical oncology concern. GHK-Cu is classified as research-only and is not FDA-approved for any indication.

GHK-Cu works at the gene expression level. Gene expression data analyzed by Pickart's group show it raises or lowers the activity of at least 4,000 human genes, suppressing some destructive pathways, when human cells are exposed to the peptide [1]. That's not a vague claim; the gene list is published and includes collagen I, III, and V, elastin, decorin (the scaffolding protein collagen needs to organize correctly), and antioxidant-related genes (Pickart and colleagues, Cosmetics 2015). The copper(II) ion is load-bearing. Without it, the tripeptide GHK has limited biological activity. Copper activates lysyl oxidase, an enzyme required for collagen and elastin crosslinking. It also supports superoxide dismutase activity, which ties into the antioxidant gene data. At the tissue level, GHK-Cu attracts both immune cells and endothelial cells to wound sites. This dual recruitment accelerates debris clearance and new blood vessel formation (angiogenesis). Pickart and Margolina described this in a 2008 review [4] as a "reset" toward a younger tissue repair program. Recent work has extended these findings. Bian and colleagues showed GHK-Cu binds PRDX6 and eases lung fibrosis in silicosis mice (Redox Biology, 2024) [2]. A 2025 mouse study found it eased DSS-induced colitis, with SIRT1/STAT3 signaling implicated [5]. The peptide's reach keeps expanding, but the core mechanism remains the same: copper-dependent gene modulation that shifts tissue toward repair.
GHK-Cu benefits center on collagen production, skin rejuvenation, and wound healing.

Collagen I, III, and V synthesis all increase in fibroblast cultures exposed to GHK-Cu, confirmed by Maquart and colleagues in the original 1988 study [6]. That's the structural backbone of firmer, younger-looking skin.

Community users consistently report visible fine line reduction and improved skin texture by weeks four to six. Over 100 Reddit threads in r/Peptides describe this as the single most reproducible outcome.

Wound healing acceleration is both the oldest and best-supported benefit. Small cuts, post-surgical incisions, and acne scarring heal faster in both topical trials (n = 41 to 71) and community reports.

Hair shedding decreases within four to six weeks for some users, with early regrowth at the temples or crown reported by week eight to sixteen. Published evidence is limited to follicle-level in vitro data, but user consistency is high.

GHK-Cu's antioxidant effects come from lab and animal studies so far. Pickart's 2012 review [3] describes that antioxidant action and the peptide's high affinity for copper ions. A 2015 follow-up from the same group in Cosmetics proposes changes in antioxidant-related genes as the reason.

Newer research points to anti-fibrotic potential beyond skin. In the 2024 silicosis study [2], GHK-Cu protected mouse lung tissue by binding PRDX6; patients with silicosis also had lower plasma GHK than controls.
Partially Aligned
Scientific Evidence
Based on 16 key studies · Research only
Preclinical evidence is strong for collagen stimulation, wound healing, and gene expression modulation (at least 4,000 human genes, up or down).
Dosing studied: Topical: 1–3% concentration. Injectable (community): 0.5–3 mg/day SubQ. No clinical trial establishes an injectable dose range for humans.

Human clinical data is limited to small topical cosmetic trials. No human RCTs for injectable route exist. 2024–2025 mouse studies expanded applications to pulmonary protection [2] and colitis [5]. Core collagen and elastin mechanisms are well-validated in vitro and in animal models.
Key Study

Pickart et al.: multiple landmark studies on GHK-Cu gene expression modulation (PMID 29986520, 26236730). Most recent: PMID 38879894 (Bian Y et al., Redox Biology, Sep 2024): GHK-Cu attenuates lung fibrosis in silicosis mice via PRDX6; includes plasma GHK data from 15 patients and 11 controls.
Limitations

No human RCTs for injectable route. Topical clinical trials are small (n=41–71), non-blinded, or lack placebo arms. Nearly all mechanistic data is in vitro or murine. Skin penetration of topical GHK-Cu is limited due to hydrophilicity: liposomal delivery unmeasured (PMID 39795193). Pro-angiogenic activity raises theoretical oncology concern (NCI) that is unresolved in humans.
Community Experience
Highly positive community reception.
Community dosing: 1–2 mg/day SubQ for injectable; 1–3% topical. Most users start at 0.5–1 mg/day and titrate up.

Consistently rated one of the most tolerated anti-aging peptides. Skin texture improvement at 4–6 weeks is the most reproducible reported outcome. Hair regrowth and wound healing are common secondary uses. Topical overuse ("copper uglies") is the most-discussed adverse pattern.

Science and community agree on core benefits (collagen, wound healing, skin rejuvenation) and the topical route. Divergence exists on injectable dosing: community doses 1–3 mg/day SubQ without a published human dose-finding trial to support any specific number. Community primarily uses injectable for systemic anti-aging while published research focuses on topical and localized wound healing. Pro-angiogenic concern is under-discussed in community protocols.

The blue-green color when you reconstitute is not contamination. It's the copper(II) ion doing exactly what it should. If your solution is colorless after proper reconstitution, that's actually the problem: copper may have dissociated, and potency drops with it. Reconstitution math for common vial sizes: a 5 mg vial plus 2 mL bacteriostatic water gives you 2,500 mcg/mL. A 1 mg dose (1,000 mcg) equals 0.4 mL, which is 40 units on a U-100 insulin syringe. For the 50 mg vial plus 5 mL bacteriostatic water, you get 10,000 mcg/mL; a 1 mg dose is just 0.1 mL or 10 units. Store reconstituted vials in a dark refrigerator. Copper ions are photosensitive. Expect two to three weeks of usable shelf life. Start at 500 mcg/day for injectable and titrate up over two weeks. Evening injection is the community standard. Rotate abdominal sites and don't hit the same spot more than once per week; lipodystrophy from poor rotation is a real and visible consequence.
Cycling Protocol
Cycle 4-8 weeks for injectable use. Topical application can be used continuously without cycling.
GHK-Cu Cycle

Injectable GHK-Cu cycling serves two purposes: (1) copper accumulation management: daily parenteral copper peptide adds measurable systemic copper load, and continuous long-term use without monitoring creates theoretical accumulation risk; (2) pathway sensitivity: GHK-Cu raises or lowers the activity of at least 4,000 human genes and activates multiple repair pathways; periodic off cycles are speculated to maintain sensitivity, though no human data confirms desensitization occurs. Topical GHK-Cu at ≤3% does not require cycling due to minimal systemic copper absorption.
Diminishing skin improvement response after 6–8 weeks of continuous use
Injection site burning or metallic taste worsening rather than improving over time
Serum copper trending toward high-normal (>120 mcg/dL) on lab monitoring
Nausea or GI discomfort developing mid-cycle at previously tolerated doses

Standard systemic: 0.5–2 mg/day. Peri-target SubQ (near scalp for hair, face perimeter for skin) uses same dose with smaller volume and finer needle (31G).

Avoid
Zinc supplements >50 mg/day
Competitive inhibition at copper transport sites. High-dose zinc displaces copper in transporter binding, reducing GHK-Cu cellular uptake and bioavailability.

The most serious concern with GHK-Cu is its pro-angiogenic activity. The NCI flagged this years ago: a peptide that promotes new blood vessel formation could, in theory, support tumor vascularization. No human case has confirmed this, but no study has ruled it out either. Anyone with an active malignancy should not use GHK-Cu without oncologist clearance. Copper toxicity is the second concern worth taking seriously. Continuous long-term use without lab monitoring creates an accumulation risk. Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis, and any copper metabolism disorder are absolute contraindications. Symptoms of copper excess include nausea, metallic taste, and jaundice; if these appear, stop immediately and get serum copper checked. Published side effects in topical trials are mild. Skin irritation, redness, and occasional contact sensitivity at higher concentrations. The more interesting adverse pattern comes from the community: "copper uglies." This is paradoxical skin worsening (sagging, accelerated wrinkling) caused by MMP-1 matrix metalloproteinase upregulation outpacing collagen synthesis. It happens most often with topical overuse or aggressive post-microneedling application. The fix is simple: drop to 1% concentration and wait 48 to 72 hours after microneedling before applying. Injectable side effects are dominated by injection site reactions. Burning and stinging from the copper ions is the number one complaint in community threads. Diluting with more bacteriostatic water, using a 31-gauge needle, and applying a cold compress for 60 seconds post-injection helps. Site rotation matters; no location should get more than one injection per week. Poor rotation leads to lipodystrophy (localized fat atrophy), which is harder to reverse than it sounds. At doses above 1.5 mg/day, some users report nausea and metallic taste. These are dose-dependent and resolve with reduction. Reconstituted stability is limited to two to three weeks refrigerated. Potency drops 15 to 30% by week four according to community tracking. The mcg versus mg calculation error is a real hazard for beginners; GHK-Cu vials are labeled in mg but doses are discussed in mcg. 1 mg equals 1,000 mcg. Getting this wrong by a factor of 1,000 is not theoretical; it's the most common beginner mistake in the community. Contraindications: Wilson's disease or copper metabolism disorders. Known hypersensitivity to GHK-Cu or copper compounds. Pregnancy or breastfeeding (no safety data). Hemochromatosis. Active malignancy without oncologist clearance. Severe kidney or liver dysfunction. Drug interactions: copper-chelating agents (penicillamine, trientine) reduce bioavailability by 60 to 80%. Zinc above 50 mg/day competes at copper transport sites. High-concentration topical vitamin C (15%+) chelates copper; separate application by two or more hours. Immunosuppressants may interact with the healing response; consult a prescriber.
Common Issues & Solutions
Blue-green solution is NORMAL: intact copper(II)-peptide complex. A colorless solution may indicate copper dissociation and reduced potency. Do not discard blue-green vials.

Injection site burning/copper sting: reduce dose by 50% and dilute with more BAC water; use 31G needle; apply cold compress 60 seconds post-injection. Persistent site reactions indicate inadequate rotation (no site should receive >1 injection/week).

mcg/mg calculation error: GHK-Cu research vials are labeled in mg (5 mg, 50 mg); doses are discussed in mcg. 1 mg = 1,000 mcg. At 5mg vial + 2mL BAC water = 2,500 mcg/mL; a 1 mg dose = 0.4 mL = 40 IU on U100 syringe. Verify concentration calculation before every new vial.

"Copper uglies" from topical overuse: paradoxical skin worsening (sagging, wrinkling) caused by MMP-1 upregulation outpacing collagen synthesis at high concentrations or immediately post-microneedling. Fix: reduce to 1% concentration, wait 48–72 hours after microneedling before applying, space to once daily.

No response by week 6 (injectable): confirm proper SubQ depth (not intradermal: intradermal causes welts and poor absorption), verify reconstituted concentration, and rule out zinc supplement competition (>50 mg/day zinc blocks copper transport).

GHK-Cu: Product Quality medium risk

GHK-Cu is a simple tripeptide (Gly-His-Lys + Cu²⁺) that is relatively straightforward to synthesize, reducing complex adulterant risk. However, injectable research-grade GHK-Cu is not produced under sterile conditions (not USP 797 compliant), creating endotoxin and sterility risks. The compounding pharmacy channel splits by route: injectable GHK-Cu is listed as withdrawn from Category 2 (FDA page current as of April 22, 2026) with no compounding access today (no FDA rule has added it to the 503A bulks list), while non-injectable GHK-Cu is back on FDA's 503A Category 1 list as of May 14, 2026. The mcg/mg dosing confusion and topical "copper uglies" risk are behavioral quality risks.

GHK-Cu is classified as a research chemical in the United States. It has no FDA approval for any indication. Sale is permitted for in vitro research purposes only; "not for human consumption" labeling is standard on research-grade products. FDA splits GHK-Cu by route. Injectable GHK-Cu was on the FDA Category 2 list until its nominators withdrew it; FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026) lists it as withdrawn, and no FDA rule has added injectable GHK-Cu to the 503A bulks list, so compounding pharmacies cannot use it for injection today. Non-injectable GHK-Cu is back on FDA's 503A Category 1 list (substances under evaluation) as of May 14, 2026, after one nominator kept that part of its nomination. FDA says it intends to consult PCAC on GHK-Cu before the end of February 2027. GHK-Cu is not on the WADA prohibited substances list as of 2026. Topical GHK-Cu products are sold as cosmetic ingredients (copper tripeptide-1 per INCI) and face fewer regulatory restrictions. They do not require a prescription. Injectable research-grade GHK-Cu is lyophilized powder without sterility or endotoxin testing. This content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before using any peptide product.
Evidence grade: Small human studies only (Peptide Evidence Gap, October 2026)

faqs.q: My reconstituted GHK-Cu is blue-green: is it still good?
faqs.a: Yes, that blue-green color is actually a good sign. It means the copper-peptide complex is intact. A colorless solution could actually indicate copper dissociation, which would mean reduced potency. The color comes from the copper(II) ion coordinated to the peptide.

faqs.q: Can I inject GHK-Cu directly into my face or scalp?
faqs.a: Perilesional injections near the target area are used clinically for wound healing and sometimes near the scalp for hair regrowth. But copper irritation is more pronounced at highly vascularized or thin-skinned sites. Most protocols use abdominal SC for systemic effects. Peri-target injection adds localized benefit but expect more site reactions.

faqs.q: How long does reconstituted GHK-Cu last?
faqs.a: Community consensus is 2-3 weeks refrigerated if you used sterile reconstitution technique. Some users report 15-30% potency loss by week 4. Keep it protected from light and don't freeze it.

faqs.q: Do I need to cycle GHK-Cu or can I use it continuously?
faqs.a: Depends on the route. Topical formulations can be used continuously since the systemic copper load is minimal. Injectable should be cycled; 8 weeks on, 4 weeks off; to avoid potential copper accumulation and maintain receptor sensitivity.

faqs.q: Any interaction with TRT or DHT blockers?
faqs.a: No documented pharmacokinetic interaction. GHK-Cu raises or lowers the expression of at least 4,000 human genes, and some community discussions on ExcelMale explore whether that overlaps with androgen pathways. But it's theoretical. No clinical data supports adjusting either compound when using both.

GHK-Cu earns a B on the Peptide Schedule safety scale. The human data are small topical skin studies; no human study has tested it alone as an injection. The main caution is its pro-angiogenic activity, which the NCI flagged as a theoretical concern for anyone with an active malignancy. Long-term injectable use without serum copper monitoring carries an accumulation risk. Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis, and active cancer without oncologist clearance are absolute contraindications.

faqs.q: What is the recommended GHK-Cu dosage?
faqs.a: GHK-Cu dosing varies by experience level. Beginners typically start at 1 mg daily, moderate users at 2 mg daily, and aggressive protocols use 3 mg daily.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of GHK-Cu?
faqs.a: The half-life of GHK-Cu is ~1 hour. This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: Three amino acids and a copper ion. That's the entire structure of the GHK-Cu peptide, a copper tripeptide the body already produces but loses roughly 60% of by age 60.

notes.text: No validated human half-life has been published for GHK-Cu; the figure here is an estimate. Each 1 mg of GHK-Cu contains about 0.16 mg of copper.
WADA does not name GHK-Cu, but its S0 rule bans substances not approved for human therapeutic use, which may cover injectable GHK-Cu. Tested athletes should check with their anti-doping agency.
